content: Individuals diagnosed with asthma are more likely to experience anxiety and depression compared to the general population. These psychological conditions are associated with poorer asthma control, reduced adherence to prescribed medications, and worse overall health outcomes. Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) has been proposed as a potential intervention to address these psychological issues, with the aim of improving the quality of life for individuals with asthma, reducing the risk of exacerbations, and enhancing asthma control. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the efficacy of CBT in comparison to usual care for individuals with asthma. The search for relevant studies included databases such as the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP). Additional sources included reference lists of primary studies and review articles, as well as direct contact with authors for unpublished data. The most recent search was completed in August 2016. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared any form of cognitive behavioural intervention to usual care or no intervention. Eligible studies involved adults or adolescents with asthma, regardless of whether they had comorbid anxiety or depression. Studies were included regardless of whether they were published in full, as abstracts, or as unpublished data. Two or more reviewers independently screened the search results, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias in the included studies. Data were analyzed using odds ratios (ORs) for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences (MDs) or standardized mean differences (SMDs) for continuous outcomes, depending on the variability of measurement scales across studies. A random-effects model was used for all analyses. The primary outcomes of interest were asthma-related quality of life and exacerbations requiring at least a course of oral corticosteroids. The quality of evidence for all outcomes was assessed using the GRADE approach, and findings were summarized in a 'Summary of findings' table. The review included nine RCTs involving a total of 407 adults with asthma. No studies included adolescents under the age of 18. The sample sizes of the studies ranged from 10 to 94 participants, with a median of 40 participants per study. The mean age of participants ranged from 39 to 53 years. Most study populations had persistent asthma, although the severity of asthma and diagnostic criteria varied across studies. Three studies specifically recruited participants with psychological symptoms, but the criteria for inclusion varied. The CBT interventions ranged from 4 to 15 sessions, and primary outcomes were measured at an average of 3 months, with a range of 1.2 to 12 months. Participants who received CBT demonstrated improved scores on the Asthma Quality of Life Questionnaire (AQLQ) compared to those receiving usual care (MD 0.55, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.17 to 0.93; 214 participants; 6 studies; I² = 53%). Improvements in asthma control were also observed (SMD -0.98, 95% CI -1.76 to -0.20; 95 participants; 3 studies; I² = 68%). The improvement in AQLQ scores appeared to persist up to one year after treatment, but the evidence was of low quality and should be interpreted cautiously. Data on asthma exacerbations requiring oral corticosteroids were inconsistently reported, preventing a meta-analysis for this outcome. Anxiety scores showed a benefit of CBT compared to usual care (SMD -0.38, 95% CI -0.73 to -0.03), although the results depended on the specific analysis used. For depression, the confidence intervals included no significant difference between CBT and usual care, whether measured as a change from baseline (SMD -0.33, 95% CI -0.70 to 0.05) or as endpoint scores (SMD -0.41, 95% CI -0.87 to 0.05). Similarly, no significant difference was observed in medication adherence (MD -1.40, 95% CI -2.94 to 0.14; 23 participants; 1 study; I² = 0%). Subgroup analyses for the AQLQ outcome did not reveal clear differences based on the format of CBT (individual vs. group), baseline psychological status, or the specific CBT model used. The small number of studies and the variability in study designs, populations, and intervention characteristics limited the ability to draw definitive conclusions about these potential moderating factors. The inability to blind participants and investigators to group allocation introduced a significant risk of bias. Overall, the evidence was of low quality, and confidence in the results was limited. In conclusion, for adults with persistent asthma, CBT may improve quality of life, asthma control, and anxiety levels compared to usual care. However, the evidence is limited by risks of bias, imprecision, and inconsistency. There is insufficient evidence regarding the effects of CBT on asthma exacerbations, unscheduled healthcare visits, depression, and medication adherence. Additionally, there is significant variability in how CBT is delivered and what constitutes usual care, making it unclear what the most effective method of CBT delivery might be. Further research is needed to determine the optimal format, delivery method, and target population for CBT in individuals with asthma. Currently, there is no evidence to support the use of CBT in adolescents with asthma.
